title: Part I: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm: Retirement/Death of a Partner

topics.title: Amount due to a retiring or deceased partner

learn.hook: A senior partner of a Chennai textile firm retires after 25 years. What exactly should his cheque say? Let's build the figure line by line.
points: Amount due = credit balance of capital (and current) account, plus his share of goodwill, reserves and accumulated profits, revaluation profit, profit up to the date of retirement/death, interest on capital and any salary/commission due.

Deduct: drawings, interest on drawings, his share of revaluation loss, accumulated losses (debit balance of P&L) and fictitious items (e.g. advertisement suspense), and any debit balance of his current account.
All these adjustments are posted to his capital account; its final balance is the amount payable.
The same rules apply on death; the amount is then payable to the deceased partner's executors.

example.q: C retires. Capital ₹1,00,000; share of goodwill ₹30,000; share of reserve ₹12,000; revaluation profit share ₹6,000; profit till retirement ₹8,000; interest on capital ₹2,000; drawings ₹15,000; interest on drawings ₹500. Amount due?

learn.reallife: Just as a retiring government employee receives a final settlement that adds gratuity and leave encashment and subtracts dues, a retiring partner's dues are added and subtracted item by item.

quiz.explain: Drawings were already taken out of the firm, so they reduce his dues.
quiz.mistake: Treats drawings as an addition

options: His share of advertisement suspense
Interest on his drawings

quiz.explain: Revaluation profit belongs to all old partners, including the retiring one.
quiz.mistake: Confuses gains with losses

quiz.mistake: Adds the revaluation loss or advertisement suspense

quiz.q: The retiring partner's share in the debit balance of the Profit and Loss Account is:
options: debited to his capital account
credited to his capital account
borne only by continuing partners
ignored
quiz.explain: Accumulated losses are borne by all partners in the old ratio, including the retiring one.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the retiring partner escapes past losses

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Interest on drawings is deducted from the amount due to a retiring partner.
Reason (R): Interest on drawings is a charge on the partner in favour of the firm.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Because the partner owes this interest to the firm, it reduces his dues.
quiz.mistake: Thinks interest on drawings is earned by the partner

quiz.q: The final amount payable to a retiring partner is:
options: his opening capital only
his capital plus the firm's total reserve
the balance of his capital account after all adjustments
his share of the firm's total assets at book value
quiz.explain: Every adjustment is posted to his capital account; its closing balance is what he is owed.
quiz.mistake: Ignores goodwill, revaluation and reserve adjustments

quiz.q: A retiring partner's current account has a debit balance of ₹5,000 and his capital is ₹80,000 (fixed). Other adjustments add ₹20,000. Amount due:
quiz.explain: A debit balance in the current account reduces his dues: 80,000 + 20,000 − 5,000.
quiz.mistake: Treats the debit balance as a credit

teach.ask: Gappu is retiring from his firm. Explain how his final dues are calculated.
teach.praise: Perfect! Add capital, goodwill, reserves, revaluation profit and profit till date; deduct drawings and losses.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: what gets subtracted from his capital before he is paid?

topics.title: New ratio and gaining ratio on retirement

learn.hook: When a partner leaves, his slice of the cake is shared by those who stay. How much extra does each one get?
points: New share of a continuing partner = old share + share acquired from the retiring partner.
If nothing is stated, continuing partners take the retiring partner's share in their old ratio, so the new ratio equals their old mutual ratio.
Gaining ratio = new share − old share, for each continuing partner.
Gaining ratio is used on retirement/death; sacrificing ratio (old − new) is used on admission.
If the new ratio is given, compute gains directly; a partner may gain nothing.

example.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C retires and A and B take his share equally. Find the new ratio and gaining ratio.

learn.reallife: When a senior doctor retires from a private clinic partnership in Hyderabad, the remaining doctors split his share – exactly the gaining-ratio calculation.

items.q: Retiring share 1/5 split equally. Each gains?
B old 2/5, takes 1/10 more. New share?
Retiring 3/10; A takes 2/3 of it. A gains?

options: old
new
retiring

items.text: If not stated, continuing partners gain in their ___ ratio.
options: old
new
capital

items.text: The retiring partner's goodwill is debited to continuing partners in the ___ ratio.
options: gaining
sacrificing
capital

quiz.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C retires. Nothing is said about the new ratio. The new ratio of A and B is:
quiz.explain: When silent, continuing partners keep their old mutual ratio, 3:2.
quiz.mistake: Assumes equal sharing after retirement

quiz.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C retires and his share is taken equally by A and B. New ratio:
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add the acquired share to the old share

quiz.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C retires; A and B take his share in 2:1. New ratio:
quiz.mistake: Splits C's share in the old ratio instead of 2:1

quiz.q: A, B and C share 5:3:2. B retires; A and C take his share in 2:1. New ratio of A and C:
quiz.mistake: Ignores the 2:1 split

quiz.q: A, B and C share 2:2:1. C retires; new ratio of A and B is 3:2. Gaining ratio:
options: Only A gains; B's share is unchanged
A and B gain equally
A and B gain in 3:2
Only B gains
quiz.mistake: Assumes gaining ratio always equals the new ratio

quiz.q: In the case above (2:2:1 → A:B 3:2), A's gain is:
quiz.explain: A's gain = new 3/5 − old 2/5 = 1/5.
quiz.mistake: Takes A's new share as his gain

quiz.q: Gaining ratio differs from sacrificing ratio because:
options: they are always identical
gaining ratio is used only on dissolution
gaining ratio is new share minus old share, used mainly on retirement/death; sacrificing ratio is old minus new, used mainly on admission
sacrificing ratio is calculated on capital
quiz.explain: They measure opposite movements and are used in different reconstitutions.
quiz.mistake: Uses the two terms interchangeably

quiz.q: X, Y and Z share equally. Z retires. X and Y share future profits 3:2. Y's gain is:
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order or uses Z's share

teach.ask: Gappu's partner is retiring. Explain the gaining ratio and how the new ratio is found.
teach.praise: Fantastic! Gain = new share minus old share, and the new ratio adds the retiring share to the continuing partners.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: how is the gaining ratio different from the sacrificing ratio?

topics.title: Treatment of goodwill on retirement or death

learn.hook: The retiring partner helped build the firm's name. When he leaves, the partners who keep enjoying that name must pay him for it.
points: Under AS 26, no Goodwill Account is raised. The retiring/deceased partner's share of goodwill is credited to his capital and debited to continuing partners in the GAINING ratio.
Entry: Dr Continuing Partners' Capital A/cs (gaining ratio), Cr Retiring Partner's Capital A/c.
Goodwill already in the books is first written off among ALL partners (including the retiring one) in the OLD ratio.
Hidden goodwill: if the amount agreed to be paid exceeds his dues (before goodwill), the excess is his share of goodwill – debited to continuing partners in gaining ratio.

example.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C retires. Goodwill is valued at ₹1,20,000. Pass the entry.
steps: Gaining ratio (nothing stated) = old ratio of A and B = 3:2.
Dr A's Capital 12,000; Dr B's Capital 8,000 / Cr C's Capital 20,000.

learn.reallife: When a founding partner of a well-known Indian law firm retires, the remaining partners effectively buy his share of the firm's reputation.

games.title: Situation ↔ treatment
pairs: Written off by all partners in old ratio

games.title: Goodwill on retirement
items: A Goodwill Account is raised at full value on retirement under AS 26.
Only purchased goodwill may be recorded.
Continuing partners are debited with the retiring partner's goodwill share in their gaining ratio.
They gain his future profit share.
Existing goodwill is written off among continuing partners only.
All partners, including the retiring one, write it off in the old ratio.
If a partner gains nothing, he is not debited with any goodwill.
Goodwill is charged only to gainers.
Hidden goodwill on retirement is the excess of the amount paid over the dues before goodwill.
That excess is treated as his goodwill share.

quiz.q: On retirement, the retiring partner's share of goodwill is recorded as:
options: Dr continuing partners' Capital A/cs (gaining ratio) / Cr retiring partner's Capital A/c
Dr Goodwill A/c / Cr all partners' Capital A/cs (old ratio)
Dr retiring partner's Capital A/c / Cr continuing partners' Capital A/cs
Dr Cash A/c / Cr Goodwill A/c
quiz.explain: Continuing partners pay for the share they gain; no goodwill account is raised.
quiz.mistake: Raises a goodwill account or reverses the entry

quiz.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. C retires; goodwill ₹1,20,000. A's capital is debited by:
quiz.explain: C's share ₹20,000 is borne by A and B in 3:2 → A ₹12,000.
quiz.mistake: Debits A with his own share of the whole goodwill

quiz.q: Goodwill of ₹60,000 already appears in the books when C (share 1/6) retires. C's capital is debited, when writing it off, by:
options: Nothing; only continuing partners write it off
quiz.explain: Existing goodwill is written off by ALL partners in the old ratio: 60,000 × 1/6.
quiz.mistake: Leaves the retiring partner out of the write-off

quiz.q: C's dues before goodwill are ₹1,50,000. The partners agree to pay him ₹1,70,000 in full settlement. Hidden goodwill (C's share):
quiz.explain: The extra ₹20,000 paid is his share of goodwill.
quiz.mistake: Treats the full payment as goodwill

quiz.q: A, B and C share 2:2:1. C retires; A and B will share 3:2. Firm's goodwill ₹1,00,000. A's capital is debited by:
quiz.explain: Only A gains (1/5); C's share (1/5 × 1,00,000 = ₹20,000) is fully debited to A.
quiz.mistake: Splits it in the new ratio 3:2

quiz.q: Why is the retiring partner's share of goodwill debited in the gaining ratio?
options: Because the retiring partner chooses that ratio
The continuing partners gain his share of future profits in that ratio
Because the firm's capital is in that ratio
Because AS 26 requires the new ratio
quiz.explain: Those who gain must compensate in proportion to their gain.
quiz.mistake: Uses the new ratio by habit

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A Goodwill Account is not raised when a partner retires.
Reason (R): AS 26 allows goodwill to be recorded only when consideration in money or money's worth has been paid for it.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Self-generated goodwill cannot be recognised, so it is adjusted through capital accounts.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the rule with AS 26

quiz.q: A, B and C share 3:2:1. B retires; goodwill ₹90,000; A and C take B's share equally. Amount credited to B's capital:
quiz.explain: B's share = 90,000 × 2/6 = ₹30,000 (debited to A and C ₹15,000 each).
quiz.mistake: Credits B with only one gainer's debit

teach.ask: Gappu's partner retires. Explain how goodwill is handled under AS 26.
teach.praise: Excellent! Continuing partners are debited in the gaining ratio and the retiring partner credited – no goodwill account.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: which partners are debited for the retiring partner's goodwill, and in which ratio?

topics.title: Revaluation and reserves on retirement or death

learn.hook: The retiring partner should not lose out if the factory is now worth more, nor escape if the stock has lost value.
points: Assets and liabilities are revalued on retirement/death, and unrecorded assets and liabilities are brought into the books.
Revaluation profit or loss is shared by ALL partners, including the retiring/deceased partner, in the OLD ratio.
Reserves and accumulated profits (General Reserve, P&L credit balance) are credited to all partners in the old ratio.
Accumulated losses and fictitious assets (P&L debit balance, advertisement suspense) are debited to all partners in the old ratio.

example.q: A, B and C share 2:2:1. C retires. Building is increased by ₹25,000; stock reduced by ₹5,000; an unrecorded liability of ₹5,000 is recorded. General reserve is ₹50,000. Find C's share of each.

learn.reallife: A retiring partner of a Kochi spice-export firm benefits if the warehouse near the port has appreciated – revaluation captures that gain before he leaves.

items: Revaluation profit on retirement is shared only by continuing partners.
All partners, including the retiring one, share it in the old ratio.
An unrecorded asset discovered on retirement is credited to the Revaluation Account.
It is a gain.
Reserves on retirement are distributed in the old ratio.
They were earned under the old ratio.
An unrecorded liability is credited to the Revaluation Account.
It is debited, being a loss.

quiz.q: Revaluation profit on retirement of a partner is shared by:
options: all partners, including the retiring partner, in the old ratio
continuing partners in the gaining ratio
the retiring partner alone
continuing partners in the new ratio
quiz.explain: The change in values happened while all were partners.
quiz.mistake: Leaves out the retiring partner

quiz.q: A, B and C share 2:2:1. On C's retirement, revaluation shows a profit of ₹15,000. C's share:
quiz.mistake: Splits the profit equally among three

quiz.q: Building +₹25,000, stock −₹5,000, unrecorded liability ₹5,000. Revaluation result:
quiz.mistake: Treats the unrecorded liability as a gain

quiz.q: General Reserve of ₹50,000 exists when C (share 1/5) retires. C's capital is credited with:
quiz.explain: Reserves are shared by all partners in the old ratio: 50,000 × 1/5.
quiz.mistake: Gives the whole reserve to the retiring partner

quiz.q: A debit balance of ₹20,000 in Profit and Loss Account exists when C (share 1/5) retires. Effect on C's capital:
options: Debited by ₹4,000
Credited by ₹4,000
Debited by ₹20,000
No effect
quiz.explain: Accumulated losses are debited to all partners in the old ratio: 20,000 × 1/5 = ₹4,000.
quiz.mistake: Credits a loss as if it were a reserve

quiz.q: An unrecorded investment of ₹8,000 is found on retirement. The entry is:
options: Dr Revaluation A/c / Cr Investment A/c ₹8,000
Dr Investment A/c / Cr Revaluation A/c ₹8,000
Dr Investment A/c / Cr Retiring Partner's Capital A/c ₹8,000
Dr Cash A/c / Cr Investment A/c ₹8,000
quiz.explain: Bringing an asset into the books is a gain, credited to Revaluation.
quiz.mistake: Credits the retiring partner directly or reverses the entry

quiz.q: Machinery ₹1,00,000 is depreciated by 10% and a provision of ₹2,000 is created for doubtful debts on C's retirement. Revaluation loss:
quiz.explain: Loss = 10,000 (machinery) + 2,000 (provision) = ₹12,000.
quiz.mistake: Ignores one of the two losses

quiz.q: Why must the retiring partner share revaluation profit and reserves?
options: Because continuing partners want to reduce their burden
Because they are paid only to new partners
Because tax law requires it
They arose while he was a partner, so he is entitled to his share
quiz.explain: Gains and losses up to the date of retirement belong to all old partners.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only continuing partners benefit

teach.ask: Gappu is retiring. Explain what happens to revaluation profit and reserves.
teach.praise: Spot on! All partners, including the one retiring, share revaluation and reserves in the old ratio.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: does a retiring partner get a share of the general reserve?

topics.title: Disposal of the amount due to a retiring partner

learn.hook: Cash now, a loan to be repaid, or instalments with interest? The firm's bank balance decides how the retiring partner is paid.
points: Paid in full immediately: Dr Retiring Partner's Capital A/c, Cr Cash/Bank A/c.
Not paid immediately: Dr Retiring Partner's Capital A/c, Cr Retiring Partner's Loan A/c. The loan appears on the liabilities side of the balance sheet.
Partly paid: cash for the part paid, loan for the balance.
Paid in instalments with interest: interest on the outstanding balance is credited to the loan account (Dr Interest A/c, Cr Loan A/c); each payment is debited to it (Dr Loan A/c, Cr Bank A/c).
Interest on the retiring partner's loan is an expense of the firm, charged to the Profit and Loss Account.

example.q: C's loan of ₹1,20,000 is to be repaid in 3 equal annual instalments plus 10% p.a. interest on the outstanding balance. Find each year's payment.

learn.reallife: Much like an EMI on a car loan from an Indian bank, a retiring partner's loan is paid down with interest on the reducing balance.

games.title: Retiring partner's loan – one year's entries
items: Transfer the balance of the retiring partner's capital to his loan account
Credit interest for the year to the loan account
Debit the instalment paid to the loan account
Carry forward the closing balance of the loan

items.q: Loan ₹90,000 in 3 equal instalments: principal each
Dues ₹2,00,000, 25% paid in cash: cash paid

quiz.q: The amount due to a retiring partner is not paid immediately. The entry is:
options: Dr Retiring Partner's Capital A/c / Cr Retiring Partner's Loan A/c
Dr Retiring Partner's Loan A/c / Cr Retiring Partner's Capital A/c
Dr Cash A/c / Cr Retiring Partner's Capital A/c
Dr Continuing Partners' Capital A/cs / Cr Retiring Partner's Loan A/c
quiz.explain: His capital account is closed and the amount becomes a loan owed by the firm.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the entry

quiz.q: Loan of ₹1,20,000 repayable in 3 equal annual instalments plus 10% p.a. interest on the outstanding balance. First year's total payment:
quiz.explain: Principal ₹40,000 plus interest on ₹1,20,000 (₹12,000).
quiz.mistake: Pays only the principal

quiz.q: In the same loan, interest for the second year is:
quiz.explain: Balance after first instalment = ₹80,000; 10% = ₹8,000.
quiz.mistake: Calculates interest on the original loan

quiz.q: Total interest paid over the three years on that loan:
quiz.mistake: Assumes interest on the full loan every year

quiz.q: Amount due to C is ₹1,50,000. He is paid ₹50,000 in cash and the rest is transferred to his loan account. Loan balance:
quiz.mistake: Transfers the full dues to loan

quiz.q: Amount due ₹2,00,000; 40% paid immediately in cash; the balance becomes a loan. Loan amount:
quiz.mistake: Takes the cash paid as the loan

quiz.q: A retiring partner's loan appears in the firm's balance sheet:
options: on the assets side
as a deduction from capital
on the liabilities side
nowhere, as he is no longer a partner
quiz.explain: The firm owes him the amount, so it is a liability.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the loan disappears once he retires

quiz.q: Interest on the retiring partner's loan for the year is recorded as:
options: Dr Retiring Partner's Loan A/c / Cr Interest on Loan A/c
Dr Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c / Cr Cash A/c
Dr Retiring Partner's Loan A/c / Cr Bank A/c
Dr Interest on Loan A/c / Cr Retiring Partner's Loan A/c
quiz.explain: Interest increases the amount owed, so the loan account is credited; it is an expense.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the entry or treats it as appropriation

teach.ask: Gappu's firm cannot pay the retiring partner at once. Explain the options.
teach.praise: Great work! Pay in cash, or transfer to a loan repaid in instalments with interest on the balance.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: if the firm pays in instalments, how is the interest worked out?

learn.hook: One partner leaves with a big cheque. The rest may need to top up – or take some back – so their capitals match the new ratio.
points: After settling the retiring partner, continuing partners may agree to keep capitals in their new profit-sharing ratio.
If the total capital of the new firm is given, each partner's required capital = total × his new share.
If not given, the total of continuing partners' adjusted capitals (after all adjustments and payment to the retiring partner) is taken as the total capital.
Deficiency: partner brings cash (Dr Cash, Cr Capital). Surplus: partner withdraws (Dr Capital, Cr Cash) or it goes to current account.

example.q: After C's retirement, A and B (new ratio 3:2) agree that the firm's total capital will be ₹3,00,000. Their adjusted capitals are A ₹1,50,000 and B ₹1,40,000. Adjust.

learn.reallife: Partners of a Ludhiana hosiery firm often top up capital after a senior partner retires so the bank sees a well-funded, balanced firm.

That total is then split in the new ratio.
Surplus capital is always credited to the retiring partner.
It belongs to the continuing partner, who may withdraw it.

quiz.q: When capitals of continuing partners are to be in the new ratio and a partner's surplus is NOT to be withdrawn, it is:
options: transferred to General Reserve
paid to the retiring partner
credited to Revaluation Account
transferred to his current account
quiz.explain: The surplus is moved to his current account, keeping capitals in the new ratio.

teach.ask: Gappu's firm just lost a partner. Explain how the remaining capitals are adjusted.
teach.praise: Well done! Fix total capital, split it in the new ratio, then bring in or withdraw the difference.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: what if the total capital is not given?

topics.title: Death of a partner: profit up to the date of death

learn.hook: A partner passes away mid-year. His family is entitled to his share of profit up to that day – but the year's accounts are not ready. How do we estimate it?
points: On death, accounting is like retirement: new ratio, gaining ratio, goodwill, revaluation and reserves are dealt with, and the amount due is paid to the executors.
Time basis: deceased's share = Previous year's (or average) profit × months up to death ÷ 12 × his share.
Turnover (sales) basis: estimated profit = Sales up to death × (last year's profit ÷ last year's sales); deceased's share = that × his share.
Entry: Dr Profit and Loss Suspense A/c, Cr Deceased Partner's Capital A/c (the profit is not yet ascertained, so a suspense account is used).

example.q: Accounts close on 31 March. D (share 1/4) dies on 30 June 2025. Last year's profit was ₹1,20,000. Find his share on time basis.
example.answer: ₹7,500, credited to D's capital by debiting Profit and Loss Suspense A/c.

learn.reallife: Insurers and lawyers settling the estate of a partner in an Indian family firm rely on exactly these time- or sales-based estimates.

games.title: Basis ↔ calculation

items.q: Sales till death ₹4,00,000 at 15% profit; share 1/3

quiz.q: Year ends 31 March. D (share 1/4) dies on 30 June. Last year's profit ₹1,20,000. D's share of profit (time basis):
quiz.mistake: Forgets to apply his share, or uses the full year

quiz.q: Average profit of the last three years is ₹1,20,000. E (share 1/5) dies 5 months into the year. His share of profit (time basis):
quiz.mistake: Ignores the time factor

quiz.q: Last year: sales ₹10,00,000, profit ₹1,50,000. Sales up to F's death this year: ₹4,00,000. F's share 1/3. His share of profit (turnover basis):
quiz.explain: Profit rate 15%; profit till death = 60,000; F's share = 20,000.
quiz.mistake: Stops at the firm's estimated profit

quiz.q: The entry for the deceased partner's share of profit up to the date of death is:
options: Dr Deceased Partner's Capital A/c / Cr Profit and Loss Suspense A/c
Dr Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c / Cr Executor's A/c
Dr Cash A/c / Cr Deceased Partner's Capital A/c
Dr Profit and Loss Suspense A/c / Cr Deceased Partner's Capital A/c
quiz.explain: Profit is not yet ascertained, so it is debited to a suspense account and credited to his capital.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the entry

quiz.q: Why is a Profit and Loss Suspense Account used on the death of a partner?
options: Because the year's actual profit is not yet known on the date of death
Because the deceased partner made a loss
Because executors keep the account
Because profit is shared only at dissolution
quiz.explain: The estimate is parked in a suspense account until the final accounts are prepared.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the suspense account records losses

quiz.q: Accounting on the death of a partner is similar to that on retirement, except that:
options: no goodwill is calculated
the amount due is paid to the executors (legal representatives) of the deceased
no revaluation is done
reserves are not distributed
quiz.explain: Goodwill, revaluation and reserves are treated as on retirement; only the payee changes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks death needs no goodwill or revaluation adjustments

quiz.q: Profit of the previous year ₹2,40,000; G (share 1/3) dies on 30 September (year began 1 April). G's share (time basis):
quiz.mistake: Uses the full year's profit

quiz.q: Which basis estimates profit using the ratio of last year's profit to last year's sales?
options: Time basis
Average capital basis
Super profit basis
Turnover (sales) basis
quiz.explain: Profit is assumed to bear the same ratio to sales as last year.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the time basis

teach.ask: A partner of Gappu's firm has died mid-year. Explain how his share of profit up to death is estimated.
teach.praise: Thoughtful work! Time or sales basis, recorded through P&L Suspense, and paid to the executors.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: which account is debited for the deceased partner's share of profit?

topics.title: Deceased partner's capital account and executor's account

learn.hook: The family of a deceased partner deserves a clear, fair statement. Two accounts – his capital account and the executor's account – provide it.
points: Deceased partner's capital account is credited with his capital, share of reserves, goodwill, revaluation profit, profit till death, interest on capital; and debited with drawings, interest on drawings and share of losses.
Its balance is transferred to the Executor's Account: Dr Deceased Partner's Capital A/c, Cr Deceased Partner's Executor's A/c.
Payment to executors: Dr Executor's A/c, Cr Bank A/c. Any unpaid balance stays in the executor's account (a liability), often paid in instalments with interest.
Interest on the unpaid balance: Dr Interest A/c, Cr Executor's A/c.

example.q: D dies. Capital ₹1,50,000; share of reserve ₹20,000; goodwill ₹30,000; profit till death ₹10,000; revaluation profit ₹5,000; interest on capital ₹3,000; drawings ₹18,000. Find the amount transferred to his executors.

learn.reallife: Banks in India ask for a succession certificate or a legal heir's documents before releasing such dues – the executor's account tracks what the firm owes the estate meanwhile.

games.title: Event ↔ treatment
pairs: Dr Executor's A/c, Cr Bank A/c
Dr Interest A/c, Cr Executor's A/c
Dr P&L Suspense, Cr Deceased Partner's Capital

games.title: Executor's account facts
items: The balance of the deceased partner's capital account is transferred to the executor's account.
The executors now represent his claim.
Payment to executors is debited to the executor's account.
It reduces what the firm owes.
Interest on the unpaid balance to executors is debited to the executor's account.
It is credited, as it increases the amount owed.
An unpaid balance in the executor's account is shown as a liability.
The firm still owes it.

quiz.q: D's capital ₹1,50,000; reserve share ₹20,000; goodwill ₹30,000; profit till death ₹10,000; revaluation profit ₹5,000; interest on capital ₹3,000; drawings ₹18,000. Amount transferred to executors:
quiz.explain: Credits ₹2,18,000 less drawings ₹18,000.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to deduct drawings

quiz.q: The entry to transfer the deceased partner's capital balance is:
options: Dr Executor's A/c / Cr Deceased Partner's Capital A/c
Dr Deceased Partner's Capital A/c / Cr Deceased Partner's Executor's A/c
Dr Deceased Partner's Capital A/c / Cr Bank A/c
Dr Profit and Loss Suspense A/c / Cr Executor's A/c
quiz.explain: The capital account is closed and the liability now sits in the executor's account.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the entry

quiz.q: Executors are paid ₹80,000 immediately out of ₹2,00,000 due. Balance in the executor's account:
quiz.mistake: Adds the payment

quiz.q: The unpaid ₹1,20,000 carries 10% p.a. interest for a full year before any further payment. Interest credited to the executor's account:
quiz.mistake: Calculates interest on the original ₹2,00,000

quiz.q: Payment to the executors is recorded as:
options: Dr Executor's A/c / Cr Bank A/c
Dr Bank A/c / Cr Executor's A/c
Dr Deceased Partner's Capital A/c / Cr Bank A/c
Dr Executor's A/c / Cr Profit and Loss Suspense A/c
quiz.explain: The liability to executors decreases and cash goes out.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the debit and credit

quiz.q: D's capital ₹1,00,000; his share of revaluation loss ₹4,000; share of goodwill ₹24,000; share of P&L debit balance ₹6,000; profit till death ₹6,000. Amount due to executors:
quiz.mistake: Adds the revaluation loss and P&L debit balance

quiz.q: An unpaid balance in the deceased partner's executor's account appears in the balance sheet:
options: on the assets side
as part of the continuing partners' capital
on the liabilities side
under fictitious assets
quiz.explain: It is money the firm owes to the estate.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is an asset

quiz.q: Which of these is credited to the deceased partner's capital account?
options: His drawings
His share of advertisement suspense
Interest on his drawings
His share of profit up to the date of death
quiz.explain: Profit earned until death is his entitlement.
quiz.mistake: Picks an item that reduces his claim

teach.ask: Gappu must settle a deceased partner's dues. Explain the capital account and executor's account.
teach.praise: Very well done! Close his capital account into the executor's account, then pay the executors with interest on any balance.
teach.nudge: Gappu asks: where does the balance of the deceased partner's capital account go?
